text: You're given an array of prices, where prices of i is a stock's price on day i. You may buy and sell any number of times, but you can hold at most one share at a time. Return the maximum profit.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. The phrase any number of times is the key — so unlike the single-transaction version, I can capture every up-move? And I can sell and re-buy on the same day, so consecutive rising days are fully harvestable?
Exactly. Unlimited transactions, one share max.

Let me run the example: seven, one, five, three, six, four. Buy at one and sell at five for plus four, then buy at three and sell at six for plus three — total seven. Note that I deliberately don't hold from one all the way to six, because the dip from five to three would cost me. That matches.

Let me think about the structure. This problem reminds me of the hold-or-free state machine, the dynamic program behind the whole stock family — always correct, linear time. But here, with unlimited transactions and no fee or cooldown, it collapses into a one-line greedy: sum every positive day-over-day difference. Why that's optimal — any buy at day a, sell at day b profit telescopes into the sum of the daily differences in between. So the best I can ever get is the sum of all the positive differences, and the greedy hits exactly that.

Here's the plan. One: start the profit at zero. Two: walk from the second day, and whenever today's price beats yesterday's, add the difference. Three: return the total. One thing worth flagging — the hold-at-most-one-share rule doesn't bind. Each positive difference is a buy yesterday, sell today, so I never hold more than one share at once. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I keep the previous day's price in start. For each day from the second one on, if start is lower than today's price, I add the rise to the profit. Then start moves to today's price. One thing worth flagging — start advances on every iteration, whether or not I profited, so I'm always comparing consecutive days. If it only moved after a gain, then on seven, one, five it would stay stuck at seven and miss the plus four.

Let's dry-run the code. Seven, one, five, three, six, four — expected seven. The row that matters is the dip from five to three. Start is five, today is three, so I skip — and start drops to three. That's what lets the next day count three to six as plus three, on top of the plus four from one to five. Both rises are captured, all three dips are skipped: seven. That matches. Corner cases: one through five, all rising, gives four — the same as one long hold, by telescoping. Seven, six, four, three, one, all falling, gives zero. A single day gives zero, since the loop never runs.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — a single pass. Space is constant — two scalars. This is the cheapest problem in the stock family. Oh, one more thing — the greedy only works because the transactions are independent. Add a transaction fee, a cooldown, or a cap on the number of transactions, and the daily differences stop being independent. Then I'd fall back to the hold-or-free state machine.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You gave the telescoping argument for why summing the positive differences is optimal. You explained why the one-share constraint doesn't bind. And you knew exactly which variants break the greedy. Good work.
